ai.definition: Longevity medicine is an advanced field that focuses on using gene editing, stem cell therapies, and other regenerative techniques to extend the healthy human lifespan.
ai.howItWorks: Through precise manipulation of genetic material and harnessing the body's natural healing processes, longevity medicine aims to repair or replace damaged cells and tissues, thereby delaying age-related diseases and extending life span.
ai.problemSolved: Aging-related diseases such as cardiovascular disease, neurodegenerative disorders, and cancer, which are major contributors to mortality and morbidity in older populations.
ai.manufacturing: The manufacturing process involves complex laboratory procedures including gene editing using CRISPR technology, stem cell cultivation, and the development of biocompatible delivery systems for therapeutic agents.
ai.buildProcess: Involves multiple steps such as initial genetic sequencing, designing targeted gene edits, conducting in vitro experiments, preclinical testing, and clinical trials to ensure safety and efficacy before market release.
ai.costDrivers: High research and development costs, specialized equipment, skilled labor, rigorous regulatory compliance, and the long timeline from discovery to commercialization.
ai.lifecycleOutlook: The technology is moving towards clinical application but still requires significant validation and regulatory approval before widespread use.
ai.regulation: Subject to stringent oversight by health authorities such as FDA, EMA, and others due to the high risk involved with genetic modifications and stem cell therapies.
ai.risks: Ethical concerns, off-target effects of gene editing, potential for unintended consequences in complex biological systems, and challenges in scaling up manufacturing processes.
ai.profitability: Potential for significant economic impact if successful, but currently limited by high research costs, narrow patient populations, and regulatory hurdles.
ai.futureDevelopment: Expected to evolve with advancements in biotechnology, artificial intelligence, and data analytics to improve precision and efficiency of therapies.

glossary.def: A process that allows scientists to alter the DNA sequence in a living organism.
An area of medical science focused on replacing, regenerating, or repairing human cells, tissues, or organs to restore or establish normal function.

subsystems.name: Target discovery (hallmarks of ageing)
subsystems.role: identifies the biological processes to intervene in.

subsystems.name: Intervention platform
subsystems.role: the tools used to act on those targets.
parts: small-molecule drugs (senolytics, rapamycin-type mTOR inhibitors, metformin)
partial cellular reprogramming with Yamanaka-type factors

subsystems.name: Biomarkers and clocks
subsystems.role: measures biological rather than chronological age so interventions can be judged.
parts: wearable and functional measures (grip, gait, cognitive tests)

subsystems.name: Preclinical models
subsystems.role: tests whether an intervention actually extends healthy life.

subsystems.name: Clinical and regulatory layer
subsystems.role: turns a promising molecule into an approved therapy.
parts: trial design using disease endpoints (e.g. frailty, cardiometabolic disease)

subsystems.name: Delivery and adherence
subsystems.role: gets the intervention into the right tissue at the right dose over decades.

buildSteps.title: Map the hallmarks
buildSteps.detail: Researchers catalogue which molecular processes decline with age and which of them are causal rather than merely correlated.

buildSteps.title: Identify a druggable target
buildSteps.detail: Genome-wide screens, human genetics cohorts and studies of long-lived people point to proteins that can be hit with a drug or edited.

buildSteps.title: Screen and design molecules
buildSteps.detail: Thousands of compounds are tested in cells for their effect on senescence, inflammation or metabolism; the best are chemically refined.

buildSteps.title: Test in animals
buildSteps.detail: Interventions are given to mice, and increasingly to dogs, with lifespan and healthspan measured, not just a single biomarker.

buildSteps.title: Establish biomarkers
buildSteps.detail: Epigenetic clocks and multi-omic panels are calibrated so a change in the marker predicts a change in disease risk.

buildSteps.title: Run human trials
buildSteps.detail: Because regulators do not approve drugs for 'ageing' itself, trials target a disease — frailty, cardiovascular disease, neurodegeneration — with ageing biomarkers as secondary endpoints.

buildSteps.title: Combine interventions
buildSteps.detail: Single agents rarely produce large effects, so regimens pairing drugs with exercise, diet and sleep are tested for additivity.

buildSteps.title: Build the clinic
buildSteps.detail: Validated interventions are packaged into screening, monitoring and prescribing pathways for people at high risk of age-related disease.

buildSteps.title: Long-horizon follow-up
buildSteps.detail: Decades of registry data are needed to check that pushing biomarkers down actually reduces disease and does not raise cancer or infection risk.

prerequisites.why: clocks correlate with age but it is not yet proven that moving a clock changes disease outcomes.
senolytics, mTOR inhibitors and metformin are being tested, but none is approved as an ageing therapy.
mouse results often fail to translate, and effect sizes are small and sensitive to husbandry.

prerequisites.tech: Regulatory acceptance of ageing as an indication
prerequisites.why: without it, every candidate must be trialled against a specific disease.

prerequisites.tech: Safe delivery of gene and reprogramming therapies
prerequisites.why: epigenetic reprogramming risks cancer if it is not tightly and reversibly controlled.

pathway.milestone: biomarker-led trials of existing drugs and first-generation senolytics
pathway.unlocks: evidence on whether ageing biology can be modified safely in people.

pathway.milestone: an approved therapy with a disease endpoint that also moves ageing biomarkers
pathway.unlocks: a commercial and regulatory template for the field.
larger, additive healthspan gains than any single agent.

pathway.milestone: controlled partial reprogramming or gene editing to restore tissue function
pathway.unlocks: regeneration rather than just slowing decline — still unproven and high-risk.

pathway.milestone: preventive longevity medicine integrated into routine care
pathway.unlocks: age-related disease pushed later in life across whole populations.
